items.stem: How did Wilson's idealism conflict with the realities of the Treaty of Versailles?
items.stemEs: ¿Cómo entró en conflicto el idealismo de Wilson con las realidades del Tratado de Versalles?

choices.text: Germany promised to warn ships before attacking after the Sussex was torpedoed
choices.textEs: No hubo diferencia entre su visión y el tratado final

choices.text: Practical politics and national interests limited the implementation of Wilson's ideals
choices.textEs: El tratado implementó perfectamente todos sus principios

choices.text: The United States emerged as a major world power despite rejecting the League of Nations
choices.textEs: Wilson apoyó medidas punitivas contra Alemania

choices.text: His Fourteen Points emphasized fair peace, but the treaty harshly punished Germany
choices.textEs: Sus Catorce Puntos enfatizaron paz justa, pero el tratado castigó duramente a Alemania

items.explanation: His Fourteen Points emphasized fair peace, but the treaty harshly punished Germany, and wilson called for open diplomacy, freedom of the seas, reduced armaments, self-determination, and a League of Nations. Choice B talks about practical politics and national interests limited the implementation of Wilson's ideals, but that describes a different law or court ruling, not the main idea in the question; Choice A talks about germany promised to warn ships before attacking after the Sussex was torpedoed, but that describes the Sussex Pledge, not the main idea in the question. It also shows how difficult it was to turn wartime ideals into a stable postwar peace.
items.explanationEs: Wilson quería "paz sin victoria" y autodeterminación, pero Francia y Gran Bretaña exigieron venganza. El tratado final impuso reparaciones aplastantes y culpa de guerra a Alemania, contradiciendo la visión idealista de Wilson y plantando semillas para la Segunda Guerra Mundial.

items.stem:
Read the following excerpt from President Woodrow Wilson's Address to Congress Requesting a Declaration of War, April 2, 1917 (Bryan, William Jennings, ed., Republic or Empire (1899), public domain — public domain):

"It is a fearful thing to lead this great peaceful people into war, into the most disastrous and dismal of all wars, civilization itself seeming to be in the balance. But the right is more precious than peace, and we shall fight for the things which we have always carried nearest our hearts — for democracy, for the right of those who submit to authority to have a voice in their own governments, for the rights and liberties of small nations, for a universal dominion of right by such a concert of free peoples as shall bring peace and safety to all nations and make the world itself at last free."

Using this excerpt and your knowledge of U.S. involvement in World War I, construct a written argument that evaluates the tension between Wilson's idealistic justifications for entering the war and the practical, strategic, and economic factors that actually drove U.S. entry. Your argument must include a specific claim about which factors were most significant, at least two pieces of specific historical evidence, and reasoning that analyzes the gap between Wilson's rhetoric and the realities of U.S. decision-making from 1914 to 1917.
items.stemEs:
Lea el siguiente fragmento del Discurso del Presidente Woodrow Wilson al Congreso Solicitando una Declaración de Guerra, 2 de abril de 1917 (Registro del Congreso de EE. UU. — dominio público):

"Es una cosa terrible llevar a este gran pueblo pacífico a la guerra, a la más desastrosa y funesta de todas las guerras, con la civilización misma pareciendo estar en la balanza. Pero el derecho es más precioso que la paz, y lucharemos por las cosas que siempre hemos llevado más cerca de nuestros corazones — por la democracia, por el derecho de quienes se someten a la autoridad de tener voz en sus propios gobiernos, por los derechos y libertades de las pequeñas naciones, por un dominio universal del derecho por tal concierto de pueblos libres que traiga paz y seguridad a todas las naciones y haga al mundo mismo finalmente libre."

Usando este fragmento y su conocimiento de la participación de EE. UU. en la Primera Guerra Mundial, construya un argumento escrito que evalúe la tensión entre las justificaciones idealistas de Wilson para entrar en la guerra y los factores prácticos, estratégicos y económicos que realmente impulsaron la entrada de EE. UU. Su argumento debe incluir una afirmación específica sobre qué factores fueron más significativos, al menos dos evidencias históricas específicas, y un razonamiento que analice la brecha entre la retórica de Wilson y las realidades de la toma de decisiones de EE. UU. de 1914 a 1917.
items.correctAnswer: A top-scoring response makes a specific claim — such as: 'While Wilson framed U.S. entry into WWI in idealistic terms of democracy and peace, the actual drivers were a combination of economic entanglement with the Allies, German unrestricted submarine warfare threatening American lives and commerce, and the strategic revelation of the Zimmermann Telegram — making practical factors the primary cause of entry.' Evidence should include: (1) U.S. economic loans and trade with the Allies — by 1917 the U.S. had lent approximately $2.3 billion to Britain and France, creating a financial stake in an Allied victory; (2) unrestricted submarine warfare — the sinking of the Lusitania (May 7, 1915, 1,198 dead including 128 Americans) and the Sussex Pledge (1916) followed by Germany's renewal of unrestricted warfare in January 1917; (3) Zimmermann Telegram (January 16, 1917) — German Foreign Secretary Arthur Zimmermann's secret proposal to Mexico for an alliance promising the return of Texas, New Mexico, and Arizona; (4) the election of 1916 — Wilson won re-election on 'He kept us out of war,' showing that public opinion was genuinely against entry before the strategic shocks of early 1917. Reasoning should distinguish between Wilson's mobilization rhetoric (making the world safe for democracy) and the proximate causes of entry.
items.dokRationale: Student must synthesize across multiple standards and sources, constructing an strategic argument that connects US.24, US.25 through evidence-based reasoning requiring sustained analytical writing.
items.explanation:
SCORING GUIDE (4 points):
4 - Exemplary: Specific, defensible claim about the gap between Wilson's rhetoric and practical drivers of entry. Two or more specific pieces of evidence (e.g., Lusitania, Zimmermann Telegram, Allied loans, Sussex Pledge, 1916 election). Reasoning explicitly engages with the excerpt — analyzes what Wilson's language reveals about how he chose to justify the decision versus what the historical record shows drove it. Analysis is nuanced and historically accurate.
3 - Proficient: Clear claim. Two relevant pieces of evidence. Reasoning connects Wilson's speech to the practical factors but may not fully analyze the rhetorical versus actual-cause gap.
2 - Developing: Claim present but vague. One specific piece of evidence. Limited reasoning; may describe reasons for WWI entry without evaluating the idealism-vs.-reality tension.
1 - Beginning: No clear claim. Vague evidence. Response mainly summarizes WWI causes without analytical engagement.
0 - No response or completely off-topic.

KEY EVIDENCE EXPECTED: Lusitania sinking (May 7, 1915); Sussex Pledge (1916) and German violation (January 1917); Allied loans (~$2.3 billion by 1917); Zimmermann Telegram (January 16, 1917, decoded February 1917); Wilson's 1916 re-election campaign ('He kept us out of war'); declaration of war April 6, 1917; contrast between Wilson's Four Freedoms rhetoric and economic/strategic causation.
items.explanationEs:
GUÍA DE PUNTUACIÓN (4 puntos):
4 - Ejemplar: Afirmación específica y defendible sobre la brecha entre la retórica de Wilson y los impulsores prácticos de la entrada. Dos o más evidencias específicas (p. ej., Lusitania, Telegrama Zimmermann, préstamos aliados, Promesa Sussex, elección de 1916). El razonamiento analiza explícitamente el fragmento — analiza lo que el lenguaje de Wilson revela sobre cómo eligió justificar la decisión versus lo que el registro histórico muestra que la impulsó.
3 - Competente: Afirmación clara. Dos evidencias relevantes. El razonamiento conecta el discurso de Wilson con los factores prácticos pero puede no analizar completamente la brecha retórica vs. causal real.
2 - En desarrollo: Afirmación presente pero vaga. Una evidencia específica. Razonamiento limitado; puede describir las razones de entrada en la Primera Guerra Mundial sin evaluar la tensión idealismo vs. realidad.
1 - Inicial: Sin afirmación clara. Evidencia vaga. La respuesta principalmente resume las causas de la Primera Guerra Mundial.
0 - Sin respuesta o completamente fuera de tema.

EVIDENCIA CLAVE ESPERADA: Hundimiento del Lusitania (7 mayo 1915); Promesa Sussex (1916) y violación alemana (enero 1917); préstamos aliados (~$2,300 millones); Telegrama Zimmermann (16 enero 1917); campaña de reelección de Wilson de 1916; declaración de guerra 6 abril 1917; contraste entre la retórica de Wilson y la causalidad económica/estratégica.

items.stem:
Read the following excerpt from Senator Henry Cabot Lodge's speech opposing the League of Nations, August 12, 1919 (Bryan, William Jennings, ed., Republic or Empire (1899), public domain — public domain):

"I have loved but one flag and I can not share that devotion and give affection to the mongrel banner invented for a league. Internationalism, illustrated by the Bolshevik and by the men to whom all countries are alike provided they can make money out of them, is to me repulsive... National I must remain, and in that way I like all other Americans can render the amplest service to the world."

Using this excerpt and your knowledge of the debate over the Treaty of Versailles and League of Nations, construct a written argument that analyzes the arguments for and against U.S. participation in the League of Nations and evaluates the long-term consequences of the Senate's rejection of the Treaty of Versailles. Your argument must include a specific claim, at least two pieces of specific historical evidence, and reasoning that connects the Senate's decision to subsequent developments in the 1920s–1930s and the failure of collective security in Europe.
items.stemEs:
Lea el siguiente fragmento del discurso del Senador Henry Cabot Lodge oponiéndose a la Liga de las Naciones, 12 de agosto de 1919 (Registro del Congreso de EE. UU. — dominio público):

"He amado solo una bandera y no puedo compartir esa devoción y dar afecto al estandarte mestizo inventado para una liga. El internacionalismo, ilustrado por el bolchevique y por los hombres para quienes todos los países son iguales siempre que puedan ganar dinero con ellos, me resulta repugnante... Nacional debo permanecer, y de esa manera yo, como todos los demás estadounidenses, puedo prestar el mayor servicio al mundo."

Usando este fragmento y su conocimiento del debate sobre el Tratado de Versalles y la Liga de las Naciones, construya un argumento escrito que analice los argumentos a favor y en contra de la participación de EE. UU. en la Liga de las Naciones y evalúe las consecuencias a largo plazo del rechazo del Senado al Tratado de Versalles. Su argumento debe incluir una afirmación específica, al menos dos evidencias históricas específicas, y un razonamiento que conecte la decisión del Senado con los desarrollos posteriores en los años 1920–1930 y el fracaso de la seguridad colectiva en Europa.
items.correctAnswer: A top-scoring response makes a specific claim — for example: 'The Senate's rejection of the Treaty of Versailles, driven by nationalist and sovereignty concerns articulated by Lodge and the Irreconcilables, left the League of Nations fatally weakened and contributed to the failure of collective security that allowed fascist aggression to go unchecked in the 1930s.' Evidence should include: (1) Senate vote — the Treaty of Versailles was rejected twice (November 1919 and March 1920); Lodge's 14 reservations, particularly Article X (League members' obligation to defend each other's territorial integrity) as the central sticking point; (2) Wilson's national speaking tour (September 1919) to build public support, ending in his stroke; Wilson's refusal to accept Lodge's reservations led to the final defeat; (3) League's structural weakness without the U.S.: the League could not enforce sanctions effectively — Japan's invasion of Manchuria (1931), Italy's invasion of Ethiopia (1935–36), Hitler's remilitarization of the Rhineland (1936) all went unanswered; (4) the alternative path — the U.S. pursued Washington Naval Conference (1921–22) and Kellogg-Briand Pact (1928) as substitutes for collective security, both ultimately ineffective. The reasoning should directly connect Lodge's sovereignty argument to U.S. isolationism of the 1930s and the failure to deter Axis aggression before World War II.
items.dokRationale: Student must synthesize across multiple standards and sources, constructing an extended argument that connects US.27, US.24 through evidence-based reasoning requiring sustained analytical writing.
items.explanation:
SCORING GUIDE (4 points):
4 - Exemplary: Specific, defensible claim about the consequences of Senate rejection. Two or more specific pieces of evidence (e.g., Senate vote defeats, Lodge's reservations / Article X, League failures in 1930s, Washington Naval Conference). Reasoning explicitly connects Lodge's 1919 arguments to 1930s isolationism and the failure of collective security — demonstrating cross-era synthesis from Unit 3 to Unit 6 context. Engages critically with Lodge's language in the excerpt.
3 - Proficient: Clear claim. Two relevant pieces of evidence. Reasoning connects the Senate's decision to 1930s consequences but may not fully develop the chain of causation or engage with Lodge's specific language.
2 - Developing: Claim present but vague. One specific piece of evidence. Reasoning is general; may describe the League debate without evaluating long-term consequences.
1 - Beginning: No clear claim. Vague or absent evidence. Response mainly retells the Treaty of Versailles story without analysis.
0 - No response or completely off-topic.

KEY EVIDENCE EXPECTED: Two Senate rejection votes (November 1919, March 1920); Lodge's 14 reservations and Article X objection; Wilson's speaking tour and stroke (September–October 1919); Lodge-Wilson personal animosity as a factor; League without U.S. — Japan/Manchuria (1931), Italy/Ethiopia (1935–36), Rhineland (1936); Washington Naval Conference (1921–22); Kellogg-Briand Pact (1928); U.S. isolationism of the 1930s (Neutrality Acts) as the long-term legacy of Lodge's position.
items.explanationEs:
GUÍA DE PUNTUACIÓN (4 puntos):
4 - Ejemplar: Afirmación específica y defendible sobre las consecuencias del rechazo del Senado. Dos o más evidencias específicas (p. ej., votos de rechazo del Senado, reservas de Lodge / Artículo X, fracasos de la Liga en los años 1930, Conferencia Naval de Washington). El razonamiento conecta explícitamente los argumentos de Lodge de 1919 con el aislacionismo de los años 1930 y el fracaso de la seguridad colectiva — demostrando síntesis entre eras desde la Unidad 3 al contexto de la Unidad 6.
3 - Competente: Afirmación clara. Dos evidencias relevantes. El razonamiento conecta la decisión del Senado con las consecuencias de los años 1930 pero puede no desarrollar completamente la cadena de causalidad.
2 - En desarrollo: Afirmación presente pero vaga. Una evidencia específica. El razonamiento es general; puede describir el debate de la Liga sin evaluar las consecuencias a largo plazo.
1 - Inicial: Sin afirmación clara. Evidencia vaga o ausente.
0 - Sin respuesta o completamente fuera de tema.

EVIDENCIA CLAVE ESPERADA: Dos votos de rechazo del Senado (noviembre 1919, marzo 1920); 14 reservas de Lodge y objeción al Artículo X; gira de discursos de Wilson y derrame cerebral (sept.–oct. 1919); Liga sin EE. UU. — Japón/Manchuria (1931), Italia/Etiopía (1935–36), Renania (1936); Conferencia Naval de Washington (1921–22); Pacto Kellogg-Briand (1928); aislacionismo de los años 1930 como legado a largo plazo.

items.stem:
Document-Based Question: The Road to War — American Neutrality and Entry into World War I, 1914–1917

Directions: Read the three documents below. Then write a well-organized essay addressing the following question: To what extent was U.S. entry into World War I in April 1917 a response to deliberate foreign provocation versus a product of the United States' own prior choices and entanglements?

Your essay must:
— Apply SOAPS analysis to at least two documents
— Use evidence from all three documents
— Incorporate outside knowledge of U.S. neutrality policy 1914–1917
— Construct a clear, defensible argument

---
DOCUMENT 1
The Zimmermann Telegram, January 16, 1917 — U.S. National Archives, public domain (decoded and released by British intelligence to the U.S. State Department, February 24, 1917):
"We intend to begin on the first of February unrestricted submarine warfare. We shall endeavor in spite of this to keep the United States of America neutral. In the event of this not succeeding, we make Mexico the following offer to alliance on the following basis: make war together, make peace together, generous financial support and an understanding on our part that Mexico is to reconquer the lost territory in Texas, New Mexico, and Arizona. The settlement in detail is left to you. You will inform the President of the above most secretly as soon as the outbreak of war with the United States is certain..."
— Arthur Zimmermann, German Foreign Secretary

---
DOCUMENT 2
President Woodrow Wilson, Address to Congress Requesting Declaration of War, April 2, 1917 — Bryan, William Jennings, ed., Republic or Empire (1899), public domain, public domain:
"The present German submarine warfare against commerce is a warfare against mankind. It is a war against all nations. American ships have been sunk, American lives taken, in ways which it has stirred us very deeply to learn of, but the ships and people of other neutral and friendly nations have been sunk and overwhelmed in the waters in the same way. There has been no discrimination. The challenge is to all mankind."

---
DOCUMENT 3
Senator George Norris of Nebraska, Speech Opposing U.S. Declaration of War, April 4, 1917 — Bryan, William Jennings, ed., Republic or Empire (1899), public domain, public domain:
"We are going into war upon the command of gold... I feel that we are about to put the dollar sign on the American flag... I am confident that the object of the President, in asking for war, is to serve the wealthy interests of our country and not the plain people... I think we should wait patiently until the American people are willing to go into war for their country rather than for the bankers."
items.stemEs:
Pregunta Basada en Documentos: El Camino a la Guerra — Neutralidad de EE. UU. y Entrada en la Primera Guerra Mundial, 1914–1917

Instrucciones: Lea los tres documentos a continuación. Luego escriba un ensayo bien organizado que aborde la siguiente pregunta: ¿En qué medida fue la entrada de EE. UU. en la Primera Guerra Mundial en abril de 1917 una respuesta a la provocación extranjera deliberada versus un producto de las propias elecciones y compromisos previos de los Estados Unidos?

Su ensayo debe:
— Aplicar el análisis SOAPS a al menos dos documentos
— Utilizar evidencia de los tres documentos
— Incorporar conocimiento externo de la política de neutralidad de EE. UU. 1914–1917
— Construir un argumento claro y defendible

---
DOCUMENTO 1
El Telegrama Zimmermann, 16 de enero de 1917 — Archivos Nacionales de EE. UU., dominio público (decodificado y entregado por la inteligencia británica al Departamento de Estado de EE. UU., 24 de febrero de 1917):
"Tenemos la intención de comenzar el primero de febrero la guerra submarina sin restricciones. Nos esforzaremos a pesar de esto en mantener a los Estados Unidos de América neutrales. En caso de que esto no tenga éxito, hacemos a México la siguiente oferta de alianza sobre las siguientes bases: hacer la guerra juntos, hacer la paz juntos, apoyo financiero generoso y entendimiento de nuestra parte de que México recobre el territorio perdido en Texas, Nuevo México y Arizona. El arreglo en detalle se lo dejamos a usted. Informará al Presidente de lo anterior de la manera más secreta tan pronto como el estallido de la guerra con los Estados Unidos sea seguro..."
— Arthur Zimmermann, Secretario de Relaciones Exteriores alemán

---
DOCUMENTO 2
Presidente Woodrow Wilson, Discurso al Congreso Solicitando Declaración de Guerra, 2 de abril de 1917 — Registro del Congreso de EE. UU., dominio público:
"La actual guerra submarina alemana contra el comercio es una guerra contra la humanidad. Es una guerra contra todas las naciones. Barcos americanos han sido hundidos, vidas americanas tomadas, de maneras que nos han conmovido profundamente al conocerlas, pero los barcos y las personas de otras naciones neutrales y amigas han sido hundidos y abrumados en las aguas de la misma manera. No ha habido discriminación. El desafío es para toda la humanidad."

---
DOCUMENTO 3
Senador George Norris de Nebraska, Discurso Oponiéndose a la Declaración de Guerra de EE. UU., 4 de abril de 1917 — Registro del Congreso de EE. UU., dominio público:
"Vamos a la guerra por mandato del oro... Siento que estamos a punto de poner el signo del dólar en la bandera americana... Estoy convencido de que el objetivo del Presidente, al pedir la guerra, es servir a los intereses adinerados de nuestro país y no al pueblo común... Creo que deberíamos esperar pacientemente hasta que el pueblo americano esté dispuesto a ir a la guerra por su país en lugar de por los banqueros."
items.correctAnswer: A top-scoring (6/6) response argues a nuanced thesis — such as: 'U.S. entry into WWI resulted from both German provocation and American self-entanglement: the Zimmermann Telegram and unrestricted submarine warfare were genuine provocations, but Norris's dissent reveals that U.S. economic ties to the Allies had already compromised true neutrality — meaning American choices from 1914–1916 made some form of entry nearly inevitable by 1917.' SOAPS analysis for at least two documents: Document 1 (Zimmermann Telegram) — Speaker: Arthur Zimmermann, German Foreign Secretary; Occasion: Germany's planned resumption of unrestricted submarine warfare; Audience: German ambassador to Mexico, then intended for Mexican President Carranza; Purpose: secure Mexican alliance in the event of U.S. entry, create a North American distraction for the U.S.; Significance: its interception and publication (March 1, 1917) was the single greatest public catalyst for American war sentiment, because it made the threat to U.S. territorial security explicit. Document 3 (Norris) — Speaker: progressive Republican Senator from Nebraska; Occasion: Senate vote on war declaration; Audience: Senate and the American public; Purpose: oppose entry by arguing that Wall Street's financial interest in Allied victory was the real driver; Significance: Norris was one of only six senators to vote against war; his argument predicted later revisionist interpretations (Nye Committee, 1934). Cross-document synthesis: Documents 1 and 2 support the 'foreign provocation' thesis; Document 3 complicates it by arguing the U.S. was never truly neutral. Outside knowledge: U.S. loans to Allies (~$2.3 billion), J.P. Morgan as Allied purchasing agent, Lusitania (1915), Sussex Pledge (1916) and its violation, Wilson's 1916 re-election on peace platform, declaration April 6, 1917 (82–6 Senate, 373–50 House).
items.dokRationale: Student must synthesize across multiple standards and sources, constructing an extended argument that connects US.25, US.24 through evidence-based reasoning requiring sustained analytical writing.
items.explanation:
SCORING GUIDE (6 points):
6 - Exemplary: Complex thesis addressing both foreign provocation AND American entanglement/prior choices. SOAPS of at least two documents accurately — especially distinguishing Zimmermann's purpose (create Mexican diversion) from its significance (outraged U.S. public) and Norris's purpose (oppose war) from his significance (economic critique of U.S. 'neutrality'). Extensive outside knowledge. Cross-document synthesis showing Documents 1 and 2 support one side while Document 3 challenges it.
5 - Advanced: Clear thesis. SOAPS of at least two documents. Good outside knowledge. Addresses both sides of the question but may not fully develop the cross-document tension.
4 - Proficient: Clear thesis. Uses all three documents. SOAPS of at least one document. Some outside knowledge. Coherent argument.
3 - Adequate: Thesis present. Uses two or more documents. Some SOAPS elements. Limited outside knowledge.
2 - Developing: Weak thesis. Uses documents without SOAPS analysis.
1 - Beginning: No thesis. Minimal document use.
0 - No response or completely off-topic.

DOCUMENT ANALYSIS EXPECTATIONS:
— Doc 1 (Zimmermann): Note Germany assumed war with the U.S. was coming — this shows German intentions clearly; audience is Mexico via German ambassador; significance = decoded by British, released to shift U.S. opinion.
— Doc 2 (Wilson): Note 'warfare against mankind' universalizes the cause; avoids mentioning economic entanglement; purpose = justify war in the most defensible terms possible.
— Doc 3 (Norris): Note explicit accusation that financial interests drove policy; this is an argument about American agency and prior choices, not German provocation; significance = anticipates Nye Committee revisionism.
KEY EVIDENCE EXPECTED: U.S. loans to Allies; Lusitania (May 7, 1915, 1,198 dead); Sussex Pledge (1916); Germany's renewed unrestricted warfare announcement (January 31, 1917); Zimmermann decoded (February 1917), published (March 1, 1917); Wilson's 1916 'He kept us out of war' campaign; April 6, 1917 declaration; six senators against (including Norris and La Follette); Nye Committee (1934) — revisionist view validating Norris's argument.
items.explanationEs:
GUÍA DE PUNTUACIÓN (6 puntos):
6 - Ejemplar: Tesis compleja que aborda tanto la provocación extranjera como el enredo/elecciones previas de EE. UU. SOAPS de al menos dos documentos con precisión. Amplio conocimiento externo. Síntesis entre documentos mostrando que los Documentos 1 y 2 apoyan un lado mientras el Documento 3 lo desafía.
5 - Avanzado: Tesis clara. SOAPS de al menos dos documentos. Buen conocimiento externo. Aborda ambos lados de la pregunta.
4 - Competente: Tesis clara. Usa los tres documentos. SOAPS de al menos un documento. Algo de conocimiento externo.
3 - Adecuado: Tesis presente. Usa dos o más documentos. Algunos elementos SOAPS.
2 - En desarrollo: Tesis débil. Usa documentos sin análisis SOAPS.
1 - Inicial: Sin tesis. Uso mínimo de documentos.
0 - Sin respuesta o completamente fuera de tema.

EVIDENCIA CLAVE ESPERADA: Préstamos de EE. UU. a los Aliados; Lusitania (7 mayo 1915); Promesa Sussex (1916); anuncio alemán de guerra submarina sin restricciones (enero 1917); Telegrama Zimmermann decodificado (febrero 1917) y publicado (1 marzo 1917); campaña de reelección de Wilson de 1916; declaración de guerra 6 abril 1917; Comité Nye (1934).

items.stem:
Document-Based Question: Peacemaking and Its Consequences — The Treaty of Versailles and the Fourteen Points, 1918–1919

Directions: Read the three documents below. Then write a well-organized essay addressing the following question: To what extent did the Treaty of Versailles fulfill, compromise, or betray Wilson's Fourteen Points, and what were the consequences of those compromises for world peace?

Your essay must:
— Apply HIPP or SOAPS analysis to at least two documents
— Use all three documents as evidence
— Incorporate outside knowledge of the Paris Peace Conference and subsequent events
— Construct a clear, defensible argument

---
DOCUMENT 1
President Woodrow Wilson, Fourteen Points Address to Congress, January 8, 1918 — Bryan, William Jennings, ed., Republic or Empire (1899), public domain, public domain (Points I, V, XIV selected):
"I. Open covenants of peace, openly arrived at, after which there shall be no private international understandings of any kind... V. A free, open-minded, and absolutely impartial adjustment of all colonial claims... XIV. A general association of nations must be formed under specific covenants for the purpose of affording mutual guarantees of political independence and territorial integrity to great and small states alike."

---
DOCUMENT 2
Treaty of Versailles, Article 231 ('War Guilt Clause'), June 28, 1919 — Avalon Project, Yale Law School, public domain:
"Germany accepts the responsibility of Germany and her allies for causing all the loss and damage to which the Allied and Associated Governments and their nationals have been subjected as a consequence of the war imposed upon them by the aggression of Germany and her allies."

---
DOCUMENT 3
Senator Henry Cabot Lodge, Speech on the Treaty of Versailles and Article X of the League Covenant, August 12, 1919 — Bryan, William Jennings, ed., Republic or Empire (1899), public domain, public domain:
"I have always loved but one flag... but I have loved America with an undivided heart, and I cannot share that devotion, cannot give affection to the mongrel banner invented for a league... I have loved but one flag and I am not prepared to put American boys under the command of some foreign general, or to bind America to go to war at the behest of other nations without the consent of Congress... Article X I consider the most dangerous obligation that has ever been submitted to the Senate."
items.stemEs:
Pregunta Basada en Documentos: La Paz y Sus Consecuencias — El Tratado de Versalles y los Catorce Puntos, 1918–1919

Instrucciones: Lea los tres documentos a continuación. Luego escriba un ensayo bien organizado que aborde la siguiente pregunta: ¿En qué medida cumplió, comprometió o traicionó el Tratado de Versalles los Catorce Puntos de Wilson, y cuáles fueron las consecuencias de esos compromisos para la paz mundial?

Su ensayo debe:
— Aplicar el análisis HIPP o SOAPS a al menos dos documentos
— Utilizar los tres documentos como evidencia
— Incorporar conocimiento externo de la Conferencia de Paz de París y los eventos posteriores
— Construir un argumento claro y defendible

---
DOCUMENTO 1
Presidente Woodrow Wilson, Discurso de los Catorce Puntos al Congreso, 8 de enero de 1918 — Registro del Congreso de EE. UU., dominio público (Puntos I, V, XIV seleccionados):
"I. Acuerdos de paz abiertos, llegados a ellos abiertamente, después de los cuales no habrá entendimientos internacionales privados de ningún tipo... V. Un ajuste libre, imparcial y absolutamente ecuánime de todas las reclamaciones coloniales... XIV. Debe formarse una asociación general de naciones bajo convenios específicos con el propósito de ofrecer garantías mutuas de independencia política e integridad territorial a los estados grandes y pequeños por igual."

---
DOCUMENTO 2
Tratado de Versalles, Artículo 231 ('Cláusula de Culpabilidad de Guerra'), 28 de junio de 1919 — Proyecto Avalon, Escuela de Derecho de Yale, dominio público:
"Alemania acepta la responsabilidad de Alemania y sus aliados por causar todas las pérdidas y daños a los que los Gobiernos Aliados y Asociados y sus nacionales han sido sometidos como consecuencia de la guerra que les fue impuesta por la agresión de Alemania y sus aliados."

---
DOCUMENTO 3
Senador Henry Cabot Lodge, Discurso sobre el Tratado de Versalles y el Artículo X del Pacto de la Liga, 12 de agosto de 1919 — Registro del Congreso de EE. UU., dominio público:
"Siempre he amado solo una bandera... pero he amado a América con un corazón indiviso, y no puedo compartir esa devoción, no puedo dar afecto al estandarte mestizo inventado para una liga... He amado solo una bandera y no estoy preparado para poner chicos americanos bajo el mando de algún general extranjero, o para comprometer a América a ir a la guerra a petición de otras naciones sin el consentimiento del Congreso... El Artículo X lo considero la obligación más peligrosa que se ha presentado ante el Senado."
items.correctAnswer: A top-scoring (6/6) response argues a nuanced thesis — such as: 'The Treaty of Versailles fundamentally betrayed Wilson's Fourteen Points by imposing punitive terms on Germany through the War Guilt Clause (Article 231), ignoring the principle of self-determination for colonial peoples, and then being rejected by the U.S. Senate, leaving the League of Nations fatally weakened — a combination of betrayals that created the conditions for the rise of fascism and World War II.' HIPP/SOAPS analysis: Document 1 (Wilson's Fourteen Points) — Historical context: U.S. entry into WWI needed justification beyond self-interest; Allied morale was flagging in January 1918 after Russia's exit; Intended audience: Congress, the American public, Allied governments, and — crucially — the German people and occupied territories (to offer an honorable peace alternative to continued war); Purpose: articulate a liberal internationalist peace framework that would justify U.S. sacrifice and build a post-war order; Point of view: idealistic liberal internationalism; note self-determination, open diplomacy, and collective security as the three pillars. Document 2 (War Guilt Clause) — Historical context: Paris Peace Conference (January–June 1919), with France (Clemenceau) and Britain (Lloyd George) demanding punishment and reparations; Intended audience: Germany and the German people, plus domestic Allied audiences; Purpose: establish the legal and moral basis for reparations ($33 billion ultimately assessed); Point of view: Allied governments determined to punish Germany; note how this directly contradicts Wilson's Point I (open covenants) and his vision of a 'peace without victory' (1917). Document 3 (Lodge) — Historical context: Senate ratification debate; Occasion: Lodge's effort to attach reservations, particularly to Article X; Audience: U.S. Senate and public; Purpose: defeat or reservationally modify the treaty to preserve congressional war powers and U.S. sovereignty; Point of view: Republican nationalist — Lodge opposed not the idea of a league per se but Article X's automatic obligation to defend members. Cross-document synthesis: Wilson promised an open, non-punitive peace (Doc 1); the Treaty imposed a punitive peace (Doc 2); and Lodge's nationalism ensured the U.S. would not be in the League (Doc 3) — three distinct failures compounding each other. Outside knowledge: Germany's resentment of the War Guilt Clause as a cause of the Weimar Republic's instability; $33 billion reparations burden; territorial losses (Rhineland occupation, Alsace-Lorraine, Polish Corridor); Hitler's rise using the 'stab in the back' myth and the 'war guilt lie'; League's failure to deter aggression in the 1930s.

items.stem:
Extended Response: World War I and the Transformation of American Society

Using your knowledge of U.S. history, write an extended essay that evaluates the following question: How did American participation in World War I transform American society, politics, and the United States' role in the world between 1917 and 1920, and to what extent did those transformations represent a permanent change versus a temporary wartime disruption?

Your essay must address at least three of the following dimensions: civil liberties and political dissent; the African American Great Migration and its causes; women's suffrage; organized labor and the economy; immigration and nativism; and U.S. foreign policy after the war. Your argument must draw specific connections between the wartime experiences of Americans on the home front and the political and social developments of the early 1920s.

Note: This question invites you to consider the experience of Tennessee soldiers in World War I. If you choose to address the experience of American soldiers on the Western Front, consider the role of Sergeant Alvin C. York of Pall Mall, Tennessee, whose October 8, 1918 action in the Argonne Forest — single-handedly killing 28 German soldiers and capturing 132 others while under heavy fire — became the most celebrated act of American individual heroism in the war and was used extensively in home-front propaganda and bond drives. York's story also illustrates the participation of rural, working-class, and religiously devout Americans in a war that many of them had initially opposed.

Respuesta Extendida: La Primera Guerra Mundial y la Transformación de la Sociedad Americana

Usando su conocimiento de la historia de EE. UU., escriba un ensayo extendido que evalúe la siguiente pregunta: ¿Cómo transformó la participación estadounidense en la Primera Guerra Mundial a la sociedad, la política y el papel de los Estados Unidos en el mundo entre 1917 y 1920, y en qué medida representaron esas transformaciones un cambio permanente versus una disrupción temporal en tiempos de guerra?

Su ensayo debe abordar al menos tres de las siguientes dimensiones: libertades civiles y disidencia política; la Gran Migración afroamericana y sus causas; el sufragio femenino; el trabajo organizado y la economía; la inmigración y el nativismo; y la política exterior de EE. UU. después de la guerra. Su argumento debe establecer conexiones específicas entre las experiencias de los estadounidenses en el frente interno durante la guerra y los desarrollos políticos y sociales de principios de los años 1920.

Nota: Esta pregunta le invita a considerar la experiencia de los soldados de Tennessee en la Primera Guerra Mundial. Si elige abordar la experiencia de los soldados americanos en el Frente Occidental, considere el papel del Sargento Alvin C. York de Pall Mall, Tennessee, cuya acción del 8 de octubre de 1918 en el Bosque del Argonne — matar solo a 28 soldados alemanes y capturar 132 más mientras estaba bajo fuego intenso — se convirtió en el acto de heroísmo individual americano más celebrado de la guerra y fue utilizado extensamente en la propaganda del frente interno y en las campañas de bonos. La historia de York también ilustra la participación de los americanos rurales, de clase trabajadora y devotos religiosos en una guerra que muchos de ellos habían inicialmente opuesto.
items.correctAnswer: A top-scoring (4/4) response makes a complex, defensible claim — such as: 'American participation in World War I triggered transformations in civil liberties, racial geography, and women's political rights that were partly permanent and partly reversed in the backlash of the early 1920s — revealing that wartime emergency both accelerates social change and generates the reactionary pressures that attempt to suppress it.' The essay addresses at least three dimensions with specific evidence: (1) Civil liberties — Espionage Act (1917) and Sedition Act (1918) suppressed dissent during the war; the post-war Red Scare (1919–1920) and Palmer Raids extended this suppression into peacetime, suggesting the change was not merely temporary; but the Abrams dissent (1919) and eventual repeal of the Sedition Act (1921) showed limits. (2) Great Migration — wartime labor demand in Northern factories drew approximately 500,000 African Americans northward between 1916 and 1920; this was a permanent demographic shift, but Northern racism and the Red Summer of 1919 (race riots in Chicago, Washington D.C., Elaine AR) showed that migration did not produce equality. (3) Women's suffrage — wartime industrial work and the argument that women were serving the country strengthened the suffrage movement, leading directly to the 19th Amendment (1920); this was a permanent change. (4) Nativism — wartime anti-German hysteria (sauerkraut renamed 'liberty cabbage,' German-language newspapers closed) fed into post-war immigration restriction leading to the Emergency Quota Act (1921) and Immigration Act (1924); permanent change. Alvin C. York: if included, York's story should be connected to the home-front propaganda machine and the construction of martial heroism, noting that York (a devout Christian from rural Tennessee who initially sought conscientious objector status) was used as a symbol of willing American sacrifice — a constructed narrative that obscures the coercive dimension of the draft and the suppression of religious dissent under the Espionage Act.

Extended Response: The United States, Neutrality, and the Question of Entanglement, 1914–1941

Using your knowledge of U.S. history, write an extended essay that evaluates the following question: What do the debates over American neutrality from 1914 to 1917 reveal about deep and enduring tensions in U.S. foreign policy between international engagement and isolationism, and how did the failure of the post-WWI peace settlement reinforce isolationist sentiment in the 1920s and 1930s?

Your essay must draw on at least three specific historical examples spanning from the WWI neutrality period through the 1930s, construct a clear argument about the causes and consequences of American ambivalence about global engagement, and connect your analysis to specific foreign policy decisions and their outcomes. Your response must also evaluate the roles of both idealism (Wilson's Fourteen Points, League of Nations) and realism (Senate reservations, Neutrality Acts) in shaping American foreign policy in this era.
items.stemEs:
Respuesta Extendida: Los Estados Unidos, la Neutralidad y la Cuestión del Compromiso, 1914–1941

Usando su conocimiento de la historia de EE. UU., escriba un ensayo extendido que evalúe la siguiente pregunta: ¿Qué revelan los debates sobre la neutralidad americana de 1914 a 1917 sobre las tensiones profundas y duraderas en la política exterior de EE. UU. entre el compromiso internacional y el aislacionismo, y cómo reforzó el fracaso del acuerdo de paz posterior a la Primera Guerra Mundial el sentimiento aislacionista en los años 1920 y 1930?

Su ensayo debe apoyarse en al menos tres ejemplos históricos específicos que abarquen desde el período de neutralidad de la Primera Guerra Mundial hasta los años 1930, construir un argumento claro sobre las causas y consecuencias de la ambivalencia americana sobre el compromiso global, y conectar su análisis con decisiones específicas de política exterior y sus resultados. Su respuesta también debe evaluar los roles tanto del idealismo (los Catorce Puntos de Wilson, la Liga de las Naciones) como del realismo (las reservas del Senado, las Leyes de Neutralidad) en la configuración de la política exterior americana en esta era.
items.correctAnswer: A top-scoring (4/4) response makes a complex, defensible claim — such as: 'The repeated failures of American internationalism — from Wilson's inability to keep the U.S. neutral without becoming economically entangled, to the Senate's rejection of the League of Nations, to the Neutrality Acts of the 1930s — reveal that American foreign policy in this era was characterized by a persistent gap between global ambitions and domestic political constraints, and that each failed attempt at internationalism deepened the isolationist reaction that followed.' At least three specific examples spanning WWI neutrality to the 1930s: (1) WWI neutrality failure — U.S. declared neutrality in 1914 but extended massive loans to the Allies; by 1917, $2.3 billion in Allied loans vs. $27 million in German loans meant the U.S. had a financial stake in an Allied victory that made true neutrality impossible; the Zimmermann Telegram and unrestricted submarine warfare then provided the final trigger. (2) League of Nations rejection (1919–1920) — Wilson's idealism at Paris was already compromised by Allied demands (War Guilt Clause, reparations); Lodge's reservations, especially Article X, reflected genuine constitutional concerns about congressional war powers; Wilson's refusal to compromise led to two Senate defeats; the resulting U.S. absence from the League fatally weakened collective security. (3) Neutrality Acts of the 1930s — Congress passed Neutrality Acts in 1935, 1936, and 1937, banning arms sales and loans to belligerents in any foreign war; these acts were directly caused by the Nye Committee findings (1934–36) that munitions makers ('merchants of death') and bankers had pushed the U.S. into WWI; the acts effectively prevented the U.S. from aiding Britain and France as Hitler remilitarized — showing how WWI's legacy of perceived manipulation drove isolationism to self-defeating extremes. Idealism vs. realism evaluation: Wilson's idealism (Fourteen Points, League) was genuine but politically naive — he underestimated Lodge's constitutional objections and his own deteriorating health; Lodge's realism was not pure isolationism but a demand for reservations that would have preserved U.S. sovereignty; the tragedy is that Wilson's and Lodge's positions were not as far apart as their personal conflict made them appear.
